Subject: Scheduling challenge for a multi‑mode, resource‑constrained project

Team,

This memo outlines the scheduling challenge for our upcoming project and the rules we will use to build a feasible, efficient plan.

Context and purpose
We need to assemble a baseline schedule for a set of activities that must be executed under resource limits, dependency and timing constraints, and a fixed budget. Each activity can be delivered in more than one way, with different time, cost, and resource profiles. Our aim is to select a delivery pattern and start time for each activity so the project finishes as early as possible while staying within all constraints.

Execution options and work packaging
- Each activity can be performed in one of several execution modes. Faster modes shorten duration but use more resources and cost more; slower modes reduce cost and resource draw but take longer.
- Activities are non‑preemptive: once started in a chosen mode, they run to completion without interruption.
- Renewable resource use is “borrowed” while an activity runs and returned when it finishes.

Dependencies and timing
- The activities are linked by finish‑to‑start dependencies. Some links require the successor to wait at least a minimum delay after the predecessor finishes. A few also impose a maximum allowable delay, requiring the successor to start within a specific window after its predecessor completes.
- Some activities also have release dates (earliest allowed start times).
- A subset have hard deadlines by which they must be completed.
- These timing rules create coordination windows that may tighten if we choose slower modes upstream or downstream.

Resources and the safety rule
- The project draws on multiple renewable resource types, each with a fixed capacity.
- To manage risk of overload, we apply a conservative safety rule for activities that are not directly linked by precedence: if there exists even one combination of their modes and one resource for which their combined usage would exceed that resource’s capacity, those two activities must not overlap in time. They must be explicitly sequenced—one must finish before the other starts—regardless of which modes we ultimately select. This is the only resource constraint; beyond these pairwise sequencing decisions, we do not rely on a separate “at all times” capacity check.
- This policy means some tasks may need to be serialized even if certain mode choices could, in principle, fit concurrently. We will decide the order that best supports the overall schedule.

Budget constraint
- The project budget is fixed and non‑renewable. The total of the selected mode costs across all activities must not exceed the budget. Faster modes can help shorten the timeline but consume more of this budget, so we must strike the right balance between speed and spend.

What this means for our planning decisions
- For each activity, we will select exactly one execution mode, trading off time, resource draw, and cost.
- We will honor all dependency links and their minimum/maximum delay requirements.
- We will respect release dates and ensure any activities with deadlines finish on time.
- For every pair of independent activities that violates the safety rule on any resource under any mode combination, we will choose a precedence order between them to avoid overlap.
- We will keep the total of chosen mode costs within the budget.
- We will set start times to meet all of the above while reducing the finish date of the final activity as much as possible.

Success criteria
A schedule is considered successful if it meets every dependency and timing requirement, avoids overlap for all resource‑conflicting activity pairs under the safety rule, stays within the fixed budget, and achieves the shortest feasible overall completion time.
